My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline trajectory, anchored around the assumption that the asset is trading near 121–122 at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 122.1 essentially projects near-flat movement with a slight upward drift, consistent with mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts. The one-week estimate of 123.0 adds a small positive increment, reflecting typical drift assumptions and modest momentum. The one-month estimate of 124.5 extends this trajectory further, embedding a continuation of the gradual uptrend while acknowledging that reversion forces and macro conditions tend to cap outsized short-term gains in the absence of strong fundamental shifts.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 3.6 points captures normal intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, that band expands to roughly plus or minus 9 points, incorporating uncertainty around any mid-week macro data releases, sentiment shifts, or liquidity events. At one month, the interval of approximately plus or minus 19.5 points reflects the cumulative compounding of all those weekly uncertainties, as well as the possibility of regime changes in volatility itself. Implied volatility levels, recent realized volatility, and the breadth of potential macro outcomes all fed into calibrating these widths.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise inflation print, a central bank policy shift, or a geopolitical shock — could trigger sharp de-risking that breaks below the lower bound, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. A sudden liquidity crunch or correlated selling across asset classes could amplify moves well beyond what historical volatility would suggest. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push prices meaningfully above the upper bound, especially over the one-month window where there is more time for such events to materialize and compound.

Finally, it is worth noting that these intervals assume relatively stable market microstructure and no structural breaks.
